strengths: Addresses a timely and underexplored intersection: adapter-based (rather than prompt-based) personalized federated learning for VLMs, which is a natural but so-far unexplored extension of MMA to FL.

The asymmetric optimization design (local up/down projections + globally shared projection) is architecturally clean and intuitively motivated by the need to balance personalization and cross-client generalization.

Broad empirical coverage: experiments span 9 datasets covering label shift (pathological non-IID CLIP datasets, CIFAR-10/100 Dirichlet), feature/domain shift (DomainNet, Office-Caltech10), and base-to-novel generalization, which is a reasonably comprehensive evaluation protocol.

Consistent and often substantial improvements over strong recent baselines (FedPGP, FedOTP, pFedMoAP) particularly in harmonic mean of local/base/novel accuracy and under domain+label shift settings, suggesting the method does achieve a favorable personalization-generalization trade-off as claimed.
Learning curves (Fig. 2) provide some evidence of stable and fast convergence relative to baselines.
The communication-efficiency motivation (only sharing the low-dimensional shared projection) is a reasonable practical advantage of the design.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core contribution is largely a direct application of an existing multi-modal adapter architecture (MMA, Yang et al. 2024) combined with a fairly standard parameter-decomposition personalization strategy (shared vs. local components) that has precedent in prior PFL literature (Sec 2.1 cites several parameter-decomposition PFL works). The paper does not clearly articulate what is technically novel beyond combining two known ideas.

No ablation studies on key design choices: there is no analysis of (a) which components should be shared vs. local (e.g., what if down/up are shared and the middle projection is local, or all local, or all shared), (b) the effect of the bottleneck dimension, (c) the effect of scaling factor α, or (d) the starting layer ℓ for adapter insertion. These are central to justifying the proposed asymmetric scheme but are left unexamined.

No quantitative communication-cost analysis despite communication efficiency being highlighted as a key contribution; a table comparing bytes/parameters communicated per round versus baselines (PromptFL, FedPGP, FedOTP, pFedMoAP) is absent.

No variance/standard deviation reported in Tables 1-3 despite the text claiming results are 'averaged over 3 random seeds,' making it hard to assess statistical significance of the reported gains, especially where margins are small (e.g., base class accuracy in Table 1).

Results in Table 2 (DomainNet/Office-Caltech10) are very low in absolute terms (all methods below ~55%, several baselines near CLIP zero-shot level), which raises questions about whether the experimental setup/training is properly tuned for these baselines, or whether the heterogeneous domain+label shift setting is simply too difficult for prompt-based methods to be a fair comparison; more analysis/discussion is needed.

No theoretical analysis or convergence guarantees for the proposed asymmetric aggregation scheme, despite the paper citing theoretical FPL work (e.g., [70]) as related; this weakens the rigor relative to some cited baselines.
No efficiency/resource comparison (training time, memory footprint, number of trainable parameters) even though parameter efficiency is a stated motivation for adapters over full fine-tuning.

Limited baseline diversity: comparisons are restricted to prompt-tuning-based FPL methods; no adapter-based or LoRA-based FL baselines (e.g., FedCLIP, or a straightforward federated LoRA/adapter baseline) are included despite being discussed in related work, making it harder to isolate the benefit of the multi-modal adapter architecture itself versus the personalization scheme.
Minor citation duplication/inconsistency (FedPGP appears as both [29] and [69] with different venue metadata), suggesting insufficient proofreading.
No explicit limitations or discussion section addressing failure cases, scalability to larger numbers of clients, or privacy considerations specific to the shared adapter design.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and underexplored problem: combining multi-modal adapters (rather than prompt tuning) with personalized federated learning for VLMs.
The asymmetric update strategy (local up/down projections, globally shared middle projection) is a reasonable and communication-efficient design that is intuitive and easy to implement.

Experiments span a reasonably broad set of 9-11 datasets covering label shift, feature shift, and domain shift scenarios, and include both base-to-novel generalization and personalization evaluations.
The paper provides clear mathematical formalization of the adapter architecture and federated aggregation scheme.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the core adapter architecture is taken almost verbatim from MMA [38], and the main contribution is simply deciding which sub-component to aggregate (shared projection) versus keep local — a relatively incremental design choice that resembles existing shared/personalized parameter decomposition approaches (e.g., FedPer, LG-FedAvg) applied to a different adapter type rather than a fundamentally new idea.

The results in Table 1 are inconsistent/confusing: pFedMMA does not achieve the best Local accuracy and only sometimes achieves the best Base/Novel accuracy per dataset, yet the paper repeatedly claims 'consistently achieves strong performance' and 'outperforms all baselines' without adequately reconciling cases where it is clearly worse (e.g., Flowers102 Local accuracy 90.22 vs. FedPGP's 99.67, OxfordPets Local 99.85 vs 100.00, UCF101 Local 93.66 vs 96.43/95.79).

In Table 2 (DomainNet/Office-Caltech10), pFedMMA underperforms on several individual domains (e.g., Painting, Amazon, DSLR, Webcam) and the overall improvement seems largely driven by a couple of domains (e.g., Quickdraw, Real) — the aggregate numbers mask substantial per-domain weaknesses that are not discussed.

No standard deviations, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests are reported despite claiming averages over 3 seeds, making it hard to assess whether reported gains are meaningful versus noise, especially given the often small margins.

No ablation studies are provided to justify key design decisions: e.g., why only the shared projection should be aggregated (vs. other splits), choice of bottleneck dimension, scaling factor, insertion layer depth, or sensitivity to hyperparameters like α and bottleneck size.

Communication efficiency claims are not empirically substantiated — no actual measurement of communication cost/bytes transmitted or comparison to baselines' communication overhead is provided, despite being listed as a key contribution.

The related work and framing overstate the novelty by calling this the 'first' adapter-based PFL approach for VLMs, but the core technical idea (partial parameter sharing between local and global components) is a well-established personalization strategy in general PFL (e.g., FedPer, LG-FedAvg), simply reapplied to adapters; this positioning is somewhat misleading regarding the scope of true contribution.
No analysis of computational/memory overhead compared to prompt-based baselines, despite adapters typically having more parameters than prompts.

The paper lacks a discussion on scalability to larger numbers of clients beyond the CIFAR-10/100 100-client setup, and does not explore varying degrees of heterogeneity (e.g., different β values) to assess robustness of the method.

Limited theoretical justification or convergence analysis for the proposed asymmetric optimization scheme, especially given that other cited works (e.g., FedOTP, theoretical FPL analysis) emphasize such analysis as a contribution.
The paper's writing contains several grammatical issues (e.g., 'Implimentation', 'adopt a multi-modal adapter design') suggesting insufficient polish for a top-tier venue.

strengths: Addresses a timely and underexplored problem: combining multi-modal (cross-modal) adapters with personalized federated learning for VLMs, as opposed to the more commonly studied prompt-tuning based PFL methods.

The asymmetric update design (local up/down projections, globally shared projection) is intuitive and directly targets the personalization-generalization trade-off, and is communication-efficient since only a small shared matrix is transmitted.

Experiments span a reasonably broad set of scenarios: label-shift (pathological class split), feature/domain-shift (DomainNet, Office-Caltech10), and large-scale non-IID personalization (CIFAR-10/100 with 100 clients), providing some breadth of evidence.
Reports base/novel/local harmonic-mean metrics that meaningfully capture both personalization and generalization simultaneously, which is an appropriate evaluation protocol for this problem.
Clear writing of preliminaries and method formalization (equations for adapter architecture and federated aggregation are precise and reproducible in principle).
weaknesses: Inconsistent reporting of dataset count: the abstract and introduction claim experiments on 'eleven datasets,' but Section 5.1 explicitly states 'nine public benchmark datasets' and Table 1 only reports results on 7 datasets (and even lists different dataset names than those enumerated as 'CLIP datasets,' e.g., OxfordPets appears in the table but not in the text's list of six). This is a nontrivial inconsistency that undermines confidence in the reported scope of experiments.

No ablation study isolating the core design claim: the paper never compares against alternative splits (e.g., sharing all components, sharing none, sharing up/down instead of the middle projection, or varying the aggregation point) to justify why splitting specifically at the shared projection is optimal. Given that this split is the paper's central technical contribution, the absence of such an ablation is a significant gap.

No variance/standard deviation is reported despite claiming 3-seed averaging in Table 1, and no statistical significance testing is provided anywhere, making it hard to assess whether reported gains (sometimes within 1-2 points) are robust.

Several baseline results appear anomalously poor (e.g., FedOTP collapsing to ~17-36% harmonic mean across nearly all datasets in Table 1, and near-random performance in some Table 2 columns), raising concerns about whether baselines were properly tuned/implemented for this particular pathological non-overlapping class split, which could bias comparisons in favor of the proposed method.

In Table 2 (DomainNet/Office-Caltech10), pFedMMA is not uniformly best — it loses to FedPGP or pFedMoAP on several individual domains (e.g., Painting, Amazon, DSLR) — yet the narrative emphasizes only the average improvement without discussing or analyzing these failure cases.

Limited architectural/methodological novelty: the multi-modal adapter itself is adopted directly from prior work (MMA), and the shared-vs-local parameter split strategy is conceptually similar to existing partial-personalization approaches in general PFL literature (e.g., FedRep, FedBABU, personalization-layer methods), just instantiated on this particular adapter. The paper would benefit from more explicit discussion of what is technically novel beyond this combination.

No computation or communication cost quantification (e.g., number of parameters transmitted/trained, wall-clock time) is provided despite communication efficiency being highlighted as a key benefit; only a qualitative claim is made.
ResNet50 backbone is mentioned in the experimental setup but no corresponding results are shown, leaving the generality across backbones unverified.

No convergence or theoretical analysis is provided, despite the paper citing related theoretical work on federated prompt learning; claims of 'stable and fast convergence' rest solely on a single figure of learning curves on 4 (out of the full set of) datasets.

strengths: Introduces the first adapter-based (rather than prompt-based) personalized federated learning framework for CLIP-style VLMs, filling a clear gap since prior PFL-VLM work has focused almost exclusively on prompt tuning.

The asymmetric sharing design (local up/down projections, globally aggregated shared middle projection) is simple, well-motivated, and communication-efficient—only a small r x r matrix per layer is exchanged, substantially reducing communication cost relative to baselines (Table 17).

Extensive empirical evaluation across 11 datasets and multiple heterogeneity regimes (pathological label shift, Dirichlet label shift, feature/domain shift via DomainNet and Office-Caltech10), with both ViT-B/16 and ViT-B/32 backbones and multiple shot settings.

Strong and fairly consistent empirical results: pFedMMA achieves the best harmonic-mean accuracy across nearly all settings, indicating a genuinely better personalization-generalization trade-off than recent prompt-based PFL methods (FedPGP, FedOTP, pFedMoAP).

Thorough ablation studies covering scaling factor, adapter dimension, starting layer, and alternative sharing strategies (all-global vs. shared-as-personalized), which support the specific design choices made.
Convergence/learning-curve analysis and a training-cost analysis (Appendix E) provide useful practical context for adoption.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the core adapter architecture is directly borrowed from Yang et al. (2024) MMA, and the personalization mechanism (splitting parameters into locally-kept vs. globally-aggregated components) closely follows well-established PFL strategies (e.g., FedRep/personalization-layer approaches) applied to a new architecture; the main contribution is largely a combination/transplantation rather than a fundamentally new idea.

Local (in-distribution) accuracy of pFedMMA is sometimes lower than pFedMoAP or FedOTP (e.g., Table 1, Table 4), and the paper does not deeply analyze this trade-off or when a practitioner should prefer a method with higher local accuracy over pFedMMA's better HM.

Results on DomainNet exhibit large instability across settings and seeds, including a 0.00% accuracy for the Painting domain in the one-client-per-domain, beta=0.5 setting (Table 10)—this raises concerns about robustness/reliability that are not discussed or explained in the text.

No variance/error bars are reported despite claiming 3-seed averaging, making it hard to assess whether reported improvements are statistically meaningful, especially given how close some HM numbers are to baselines (e.g., Table 2 at beta=5,10 where the delta is near zero or negative).

Baselines are restricted to federated prompt-tuning methods; no comparison against other federated adapter or LoRA-based PEFT methods for VLMs (uni-modal adapters, LoRA) is included, which would better contextualize the specific benefit of the multi-modal adapter design in the federated setting.

The choice to share only the middle projection (versus, e.g., sharing down-projection or different subsets) is empirically justified via ablation but lacks theoretical grounding for why this specific split optimally balances personalization and generalization.

strengths: The paper conducts an extensive empirical study across 11 datasets covering label-shift, feature-shift, and personalization scenarios, with several ablations (scaling factor, adapter dimension, starting layer, sharing strategy) that help characterize the design choices.

The idea of splitting an adapter into modality-specific local components and a shared cross-modal projection for communication is a reasonable, communication-efficient instantiation of asymmetric PFL for VLMs, and the paper provides a clear communication/parameter-cost analysis relative to prompt-tuning baselines.

The presentation of trade-offs between personalization (local accuracy) and generalization (base/novel HM) is a useful framing, and the paper is reasonably transparent about baseline weaknesses (e.g., FedOTP's poor novel-class generalization).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core contribution is applying an existing architecture (MMA, Yang et al. 2024) to federated learning using a standard 'partial personalization' strategy (local vs. globally-aggregated parameters) that closely mirrors long-established PFL approaches (e.g., FedPer, personalization layers, shared-representation PFL). The paper does not provide theoretical justification for why the shared projection specifically balances generalization/personalization beyond empirical observation.

Results are inconsistent and in places concerning: on DomainNet/Office-Caltech10 (Tables 3, 9, 10), pFedMMA sometimes performs dramatically worse than simple baselines (e.g., 9.26% on Amazon vs. 20.34% for FedPGP, and several 0.00% entries for the Painting domain under certain client splits), suggesting instability under some heterogeneous/domain-shift configurations that is not discussed or explained.

No variance/standard deviation is reported despite claiming experiments are repeated three times with different seeds, making it difficult to assess statistical significance of the reported gains, especially where improvements over baselines are small (e.g., <1% in several HM columns).

The 'local accuracy' metric rewards memorization of a client's own narrow class set; pFedMMA sometimes trades off local accuracy for HM gains (e.g., lower local accuracy than pFedMoAP in several settings), so the headline claim of 'best trade-off' is somewhat metric-dependent and could be presented more critically.

The comparison set is limited to prompt-tuning-based FL baselines; despite motivating the work by contrasting adapters vs. prompts, no adapter-based FL baseline (e.g., an adapter analogue of FedCLIP, or straightforward FedAvg over MMA) is included as a baseline beyond the paper's own ablation 'Baseline 1/2', weakening the claim of superiority over the broader adapter-based FL space.

Minor clarity/writing issues (duplicated bibliography entries for Cui et al., some inconsistent numbers between Table 1 and Appendix Table 7, dense/hard-to-parse tables) reduce reproducibility and readability.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation spanning eleven datasets covering label-shift, feature-shift/domain-shift, and personalization scenarios, plus multiple backbone sizes (ViT-B/16 and ViT-B/32).

The asymmetric adapter-sharing design (personalizing up/down projections while globally aggregating only the shared cross-modal projection) is intuitive and communication-efficient, transmitting only a small fraction of parameters per round.
Good ablation coverage: scaling factor, adapter dimension, starting layer, and alternative sharing strategies (all-global vs. shared-as-personal) are all tested, helping justify design choices.

The paper clearly identifies and quantifies a real limitation of prior federated prompt-tuning methods (strong personalization but poor generalization to base/novel classes, e.g., FedOTP), motivating the proposed trade-off.
Reasonably strong and consistent improvements in harmonic-mean accuracy across shots and datasets in the main base-to-novel generalization tables.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the core technical contribution largely combines an existing multi-modal adapter architecture (Yang et al., 2024, MMA) with a well-established PFL strategy of splitting parameters into shared/global vs. local/personalized components (a pattern used in prior PFL work such as personalization-layer approaches); the paper does not sufficiently differentiate this combination from straightforward engineering.

Results on DomainNet/Office-Caltech10 (Tables 3, 9, 10) are highly volatile and in places implausible (e.g., 0.00% accuracy for the Painting domain in one setting, huge swings across β values), raising concerns about robustness, correctness, or cherry-picking of the specific runs reported, and undermining confidence in the feature-shift claims.
In Office-Caltech10, pFedMMA is sometimes clearly worse than baselines (e.g., Amazon domain in Table 3: 9.26% vs. FedPGP's 20.34%), which is not adequately discussed or explained in the text.

No variance/standard deviation is reported despite claiming experiments are repeated three times, making it hard to assess the statistical significance of the reported improvements, especially given the volatility seen in domain-shift tables.
No theoretical analysis or convergence guarantee for the proposed asymmetric local/global optimization scheme, despite it being the central algorithmic novelty.

Some baselines discussed in related work (e.g., pFedPrompt) are not included in the main experimental comparisons, limiting the completeness of the empirical comparison against the full space of personalized federated prompt/adapter methods.
Minor scholarly issues, such as duplicate/redundant bibliography entries (e.g., FedPGP cited twice with different years), suggest insufficient care in manuscript preparation.
